sections.h2: Who bills and who values property
sections.html:
Two Clayton County offices touch every parcel. Valuation sits with the Board of Tax Assessors. Billing and collection sit with the Tax Commissioner, who also divides the money among the county, the cities, fire services and the school board. The millage rate is not either office's call: county commissioners set the county rate and each other taxing body sets its own.

Both offices share the Jonesboro government complex at 121 South McDonough Street. Assessors: Annex 3, fourth floor, (770) 477-3285. Tax Commissioner: Annex 3, second floor, property tax line (770) 477-3311. A value question sent to the commissioner, or a payoff question sent to the assessors, just gets passed along, which costs a seller days.

Ownership and value are locked in on January 1. A house sold in October is still billed to the person who held it that January, so lay the tax bill next to the closing statement and compare.

Clayton sits just south of Atlanta, densely built, with the courthouse in Jonesboro and most of Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport inside its lines. The 2020 census counted 297,595 residents, 106,200 households and 114,038 housing units, 6.9% of them vacant. Renters edged out owners, at 50.5% of occupied homes to 49.5%.

That mix means a landlord selling with tenants in place is a common situation here, and the lease is one more thing to settle before a closing date. Part of the county lies inside city limits, so find out from the Tax Commissioner whether your parcel gets a city bill on top of the county one, because a seller's payoff has to cover both.

The Tax Commissioner describes a yearly rhythm. Notices of assessment arrive in spring or early summer. Millage rates get worked out between about mid July and mid August, and the bills themselves follow around mid September. The due date is usually in mid November, with a payment window of 60 days after mail-out. Exact dates move from year to year. The printed bill has them, or call (770) 477-3311.

If your value is under appeal when bills go out, you receive two bills. One covers 85% and falls due with everyone else's. The other covers the remaining 15% and comes due, or comes back as a refund, after the appeal settles. Request both before the house goes on the market.

Georgia adds two rules of its own. Interest begins 60 days after the bill is postmarked, and delinquent balances can draw penalties too. Anyone claiming tax was assessed in error has three years from payment to start that claim. Refunds from an appeal come after the final value is set.

The appeal clock runs 45 days from the mailing date on the notice, and only a written appeal counts. Homestead applications and other special assessment requests share that date. Filing late costs you that year's challenge. Take it to the assessors in Annex 3 or file through the online appeals site.

After the first review, the notice lists four routes.

Appeal routes after the first review
RouteWhat it can decideCondition printed on the notice
Board of EqualizationValue, uniformity, exemptions or taxabilityOpen to any owner who files in time
Nonbinding arbitrationValue onlyRequires a certified appraisal
Hearing officerValue or uniformityReal property that is not a homestead and is valued above $500,000, plus large personal property accounts
Superior CourtAs agreedOnly by written agreement with the assessors

Ask early: the assessors must hand over the records behind your value within 10 business days of a request. Bring comparable sales, plus photos of any defects an assessor could not see from the street. The rate itself is off the table, because an appeal reaches value, uniformity and taxability only.

Homestead status covers the single house you own and occupy as your main residence on January 1. Nobody can claim two. Applications go to the Tax Commissioner. File between January 2 and April 1. Anything later is held for the next year. Once approved, it renews on its own. You only have to report if you stop qualifying.

Clayton voters were also given a local base-year homestead freeze on the county-purposes value for these groups:

  • Residents age 65 or older
  • Disabled former service members
  • Unremarried surviving spouses of peace officers or firefighters killed in the line of duty
  • Residents who are 100 percent disabled

Whether your parcel is covered is a question for the commissioner's office.

A homestead exemption follows the occupant. A buyer files separately after moving in, so the next bill on the house can run higher than yours did.

Unpaid taxes lead to an execution on the property and, eventually, a tax sale. The Tax Commissioner's property portal carries tax sale notices, a bidder pre-registration form, and an excess funds claim form for owners who are owed money after a sale.

A tax sale transfers a tax deed and not clear title, and Georgia gives the former owner a right to redeem. Lenders will not lend against a house with a lien, and whatever is owed comes off your proceeds at closing. If you are behind, call (770) 477-3311 first and ask what it takes to clear the account by your target closing date.

sections.h2: Selling with a bill outstanding or an appeal pending
sections.html:
Nothing at the county level divides the year between buyer and seller. The contract and the settlement statement, prepared by the closing attorney, do that. Have the closing office request a payoff covering the county bill and any city bill. Run through this list before listing:

  • Download the current bill from the Tax Commissioner's portal and see if a city bill applies too.
  • Check for a pending appeal, which brings a second bill for the remaining 15%.
  • Confirm that any homestead exemption will be removed after the sale.
  • Keep the closing statement as your proof the bill was paid.
  • Hand the closing attorney your latest assessment notice and any appeal paperwork so the payoff request is accurate.

A sale with tenants or a repair list can still close on a cash timeline, and a cash sale skips the buyer's loan appraisal and underwriting. Compare any written cash offer with what a listing would net after repairs, showings and the wait.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to appeal a Clayton County value?
faqs.a: Send a written appeal within 45 days of the date printed on your assessment notice. Deliver it to the assessors at 121 S. McDonough Street, Annex 3, fourth floor, or use the county's online appeals site. Miss it and the value stands for that year.

faqs.q: Which Clayton County office handles bills and which handles values?
faqs.a: Bills, payments, exemptions and payoff figures come from the Tax Commissioner, (770) 477-3311. Values, notices and appeals belong to the assessors, (770) 477-3285. The assessors collect no money, and the commissioner cannot change a value.

faqs.q: Do I pay anything while a Clayton County appeal is pending?
faqs.a: Yes, most of it. A parcel under appeal gets two bills, and the 85% bill is due on the regular date. The remaining 15% is settled after the decision, which can leave a small balance or a refund.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Clayton County house that has unpaid taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The closing office pays the back taxes out of your proceeds, so ask for a payoff figure good through the closing date. If the parcel already went to a tax sale, the tax deed buyer holds an interest until redemption, so call (770) 477-3311 first.

faqs.q: Does my homestead exemption transfer to the buyer?
faqs.a: No. The exemption goes with the person living in the house. The buyer applies on their own with the Tax Commissioner, and an application filed after April 1 takes effect the following year.
